931.quote_or_event: “Trying to taste the flavor, you swallow the hook.”
931.explanation: Bhagat Namdev uses the old image of the fish: drawn by the taste of the bait, it swallows the iron hook (loh) hidden inside and is caught. For him the lure of the senses always hides the hook.
931.tie_back: This is almost exactly the Kural’s simile, where the gambler’s winnings are the bait a fish swallows together with the iron hook.
931.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 1252, Raag Saarang, Bhagat Namdev (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
931._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim via BaniDB/SikhiToTheMax; the bait-and-iron-hook image is near one-to-one, though Namdev applies it to sensual craving in general, not to gambling.

932.quote_or_event: “I have seen the world to be such a gambler; all beg for peace, but they forget the Naam, the Name of the Lord. ... People beg for peace, but they receive severe pain.”
932.explanation: Guru Nanak looks at the whole world and sees a gambler: everyone stakes their life on winning happiness, forgets the Name that actually gives it, and ends up with far more pain than they began with.
932.tie_back: The Kural’s gambler gains one and loses a hundred and never reaches anything good, and Guru Nanak’s gambling world asks for peace and receives great pain.
932.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 222, Raag Gauree Gwaarayree, Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
932._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim via BaniDB/SikhiToTheMax (ellipsis marks omitted lines of the same shabad); a strong fit on gaining little and losing much, with gambling used as a metaphor for worldly life.

933.quote_or_event: “Like the gambler losing the game of chance, you are held in the power of sensory desires.”
933.explanation: Guru Arjan tells the soul that it is losing its life the way a gambler loses at play, because the senses have got hold of it. The image is of someone who keeps playing and keeps losing.
933.tie_back: The Kural warns that the one who keeps calling stakes on the rolling dice will see his wealth and income pass to others, and Guru Arjan’s losing gambler is that same figure.
933.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 212, Raag Gauree, Guru Arjan (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
933._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim via BaniDB/SikhiToTheMax; it shares the picture of the steady loser, but the subject is spiritual loss to the senses, not money passing to other players.

934.quote_or_event: “The position of the losing gambler is similar to the deer caught in a trap.”
934.explanation: Bhai Gurdas compares the gambler who has lost his money (vit haar jooaaree) to a deer caught in a snare, unable to get free and facing ruin.
934.tie_back: The Kural says nothing brings poverty and misery like gambling, and Bhai Gurdas’s gambler stripped of his wealth and trapped like a deer is that misery made visible.
934.source: Vaaran Bhai Gurdas, Vaar 36, Pauri 3 (English translation as published on BaniDB/SikhiToTheMax and searchgurbani.com)
934._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim via BaniDB; it fits poverty and entrapment, but it is a single simile within a pauri on another subject, and Bhai Gurdas is exegesis, not scripture.

935.quote_or_event: “Says Kabeer, think of doing some good deeds. In the end, the gambler shall depart empty-handed.”
935.explanation: Kabir reminds the proud that kings, gold forts and elephants at the door go with no one, and closes by saying that a person who stakes everything on wealth leaves this world like a gambler, with nothing in his hands.
935.tie_back: The Kural says those who took pride in dice, gaming hall and skilled hands, and would not let them go, end up with nothing, and Kabir’s gambler likewise departs empty-handed.
935.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 1158, Raag Bhairao, Bhagat Kabir (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
935._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim via BaniDB/SikhiToTheMax; the empty-handed gambler matches closely, though Kabir uses the gambler as a figure for anyone who trusts in wealth.

936.quote_or_event: “Thieves, adulterers and gamblers are pressed like seeds in the mill.”
936.explanation: Guru Nanak names the gambler with the thief and the adulterer as people whose own deeds grind them, as an oil press crushes seeds.
936.tie_back: The Kural says those swallowed by the misfortune called gambling will suffer many sorrows, and Guru Nanak’s gamblers, crushed in the mill, are suffering exactly that.
936.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 1288, Raag Malaar, Malaar ki Vaar, Salok, Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
936._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim via BaniDB/SikhiToTheMax; gambling named as a cause of crushing suffering fits well, but the Kural’s goddess of misfortune has no Sikh counterpart, and Sikhism rejects such deities.

937.quote_or_event: “Like a gambler he loses and wastes his precious life.”
937.explanation: In a pauri headed ‘Wasting the life by the gambler’, Bhai Gurdas compares the person who throws away the priceless human birth to a gambler who loses everything at play.
937.tie_back: The Kural says days spent in the gaming hall destroy both inherited wealth and good character, and Bhai Gurdas makes the stake even larger: the gambler loses life itself.
937.source: Vaaran Bhai Gurdas, Vaar 37, Pauri 26 (English translation as published on BaniDB/SikhiToTheMax and searchgurbani.com)
937._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim via BaniDB; the gambler’s self-ruin fits, but Bhai Gurdas speaks of the wasted human birth rather than lost property and character, and his work is exegesis, not scripture.

938.quote_or_event: “The truth is perfect and the falsehood a loser gambler running from pillar to post.”
938.explanation: Bhai Gurdas sets truth, which is whole and secure, against falsehood, which he pictures as a gambler who has lost and runs here and there. Lying and losing at dice go together in his image.
938.tie_back: The Kural lists gambling as the vice that drives a man to lies, and Bhai Gurdas gives falsehood the very face of a losing gambler.
938.source: Vaaran Bhai Gurdas, Vaar 30, Pauri 5 (English translation as published on BaniDB/SikhiToTheMax and searchgurbani.com)
938._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim via BaniDB; it links falsehood and gambling, but it does not mention the Kural’s ruin of wealth or loss of compassion, and Bhai Gurdas is exegesis, not scripture.

939.quote_or_event: “One who works for what he eats, and gives some of what he has - O Nanak, he knows the Path.”
939.explanation: Guru Nanak’s short salok sums up two pillars of Sikh life, kirat karni (honest work) and vand chhakna (sharing). Food, clothing and standing are to come from honest labour, never from chance or someone else’s loss.
939.tie_back: The Kural says the gambler never gets clothing, wealth, food, renown or learning, and Guru Nanak names the honest, sharing path by which a person does gain them.
939.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 1245, Raag Saarang, Saarang ki Vaar, Salok Mahala 1, Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
939._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim via BaniDB/SikhiToTheMax; a positive contrast rather than a parallel, since it never mentions gambling, but it is the core Sikh answer to unearned gain.

940.quote_or_event: “as the gambler’s addiction does not leave him, So is this mind of Nanak’s attached to the Lord.”
940.explanation: In a long list of passionate attachments (the moth to the flame, the elephant to its lust), Guru Arjan includes the gambler whose habit will not let him go. He then turns the image round: let the mind cling to the Lord just as tightly.
940.tie_back: The Kural observes that gambling is loved all the more the more one loses, and Guru Arjan names that same unbreakable addiction, though he redirects its force toward God.
940.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 838, Raag Bilaaval, Guru Arjan (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
940._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on srigranth.org; matches the gambler’s compulsion, but Guru Arjan uses it as a model for devotion, and the Kural’s second half about the soul clinging to a suffering body is not addressed.
